newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian unemployment falls, poor south still suffers.
newsitem.headline: Italian unemployment falls, poor south still suffers.

text.p: Italian unemployment dipped to 11.7 percent of the labour force at the end of July from 12.3 percent at the end of April, but the disparity between the north and south remained vast, the statistics office Istat said on Friday.
Istat added that the fall was due almost entirely to seasonal factors as the tourist season moved into top gear, creating short-term jobs across the country.
"Year-on-year employment rose only in the service sector, while the performance of the agricultural sector remained negative and there was a fresh contraction in the industrial sector," Istat said.
While the jobless total eased slightly throughout Italy, the underdeveloped south still bore the brunt of unemployment, with 21.4 percent of people there looking for work.
By contrast only 6.2 percent of the labour force in the north and 9.7 percent of people in the centre of Italy were unemployed, Istat said.

Italy's centre-left government has put the fight against unemployment at the top of its political agenda and on Tuesday signed a wide-ranging labour pact with unions and employers in a bid to stimulate the job market.
The long-awaited accord included a reduction in the working week, incentives for people starting up their own businesses, tax breaks on research and encouragement for training schemes.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi promised to provide 15 trillion lire ($9.9 billion) of government funds over the next three years to help finance various projects.
Some 3.5 trillion lire of this is expected to be raised in the 1997 budget, which Prodi was due to unveil later on Friday.

Istat, which releases employment data every three months, said the total number of people in work in Italy at the end of July was 20.3 million, up 1.2 percent on April's total and up 0.3 percent on July 1995.

The army of unemployed eased to 2.69 million, down 4.5 percent on April's level. However the number of people who have been looking for work for more than a year continued to grow and accounted for 68.9 percent of the overall jobless total.
Youth unemployment was also a major problem, with 32.9 percent of all people aged between 15 and 24 without work. In the south, this figure soared to 54.9 percent.

As part of the labour pact, the government said it would raise the age at which people could leave school to 16 from the present 14 and promised to provide further education for anyone up to the age of 18.
Analysts said the move should lead to a noticeable fall in the unemployment rate.

The government is hoping to chop a further 50,000 off the jobless queue with the relaunch of a major infrastructure programme, which ground to a halt in the wake of the widespread corruption scandals of the early 1990s.
Work on long-awaited motorway links in the centre and south of Italy is due to begin by the end of the year, along with an ambitious extension of the high speed railway network.
